job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Beth Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Beth. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a finance assistant at Westmead Homes, a housing association in Bristol. I process supplier invoices, run the rent arrears report and help the finance manager, Marcus, with the monthly budget pack. I share a flat in Bedminster with my friend Abena. Lunch is usually in the park with the repairs team, because they know where the money actually goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say fine, we keep housing people and the money side stays human. To friends I'd say AI is a tool and the headlines are louder than the reality. Online I'd share a news piece with a sceptical comment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record I'm a bit relieved. I use an AI tool now and then to summarise long board papers, and it saves me twenty minutes. I'd like it to stay a helper while I learn the housing side properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and start the accounting qualification this autumn, which the association part-funds. I'd save about three hundred a month and keep using the summary tool. I'd also keep helping with my parents' shop books on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small knot underneath. My job is steady and tenants always need housing, but the money for it keeps shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your parents' shop. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad Kofi runs a small import shop in Croydon and keeps his books in a notebook. I sit with him some Sundays and move it into a spreadsheet. It's the one thing my family asks of me, and I like being useful there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries would remain even if nothing changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing associations are squeezed. Rent caps and repair costs mean budgets get cut. Finance teams get efficiency reviews even without AI. And Bristol rents are so high that I can't picture buying a flat.

say: I'd tell colleagues we keep **housing people** and the money side stays human.
I'd tell friends the headlines are louder than reality, with a sceptical post online.
think: I'm quietly **relieved**, since AI only saves me twenty minutes on board papers.
The real pressure is **shrinking budgets** at the association, not software.
do: Start the **accounting qualification** this autumn, part-funded by the association.
Save about **£300 a month** and keep using the summary tool.
feel: **Mostly calm**, with a small knot about funding at the back of my mind.
S0.quote: Housing associations are squeezed. Rent caps and repair costs mean budgets get cut.
fieldNote: Calm about AI, but pressure on **housing budgets** already weighs on her.
Helps her father with his books, which shows how she thinks of finance: **useful**, not glamorous.
Has family backing yet worries about Bristol rents.

steps.text: Start the part-funded accounting qualification this autumn
Save about 300 pounds a month
Keep using the AI summary tool on long board papers
Keep doing the notebook-to-spreadsheet job for my dad

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. It's called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should use the tools to free time for tenant visits, not to cut posts. To friends I'd say governments should fund retraining and keep unions at the table. Online I'd share the housing union's guidance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think invoice processing and arrears reports are exactly what gets automated first. Marcus already asked me to test an invoice-reading tool. My job could shrink to checking what it did, and our team of four might become three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be the one who tests the tools, so I'm part of the change. I'd press on with the accounting qualification, because judgement jobs last longer. And I'd ask about moving towards tenant services, since I like that side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for my own pay, but I watch the others. Gill (our oldest colleague, fifty-eight) does invoices all day and she's not happy about the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Gill to learn it with me. I'd show her the tool in my lunch break, because she spots wrong figures faster than I do. I'd also tell Marcus she's worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does your family come into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum is a nurse and says every job gets changed and you adapt. My dad worries more and thinks young people are being sold a story. I tell them I'm fine, and mostly I am, but I'd lean on them for rent if I had a gap.

say: I'd say use the tools to **free time for tenants**, not to cut posts.
I'd push for retraining funds and the **union at the table**.
think: Invoices and arrears reports are the **first tasks** to go, so our team of four may shrink.
My job could shrink to checking what the software did.
do: Volunteer to **test the invoice tool** so I'm part of the change.
Press on with the **accounting qualification**, since judgement jobs last longer.
Ask about a move towards tenant services.
feel: **Uneasy**; not scared for my own pay but watching colleagues like Gill.
S1.quote: I'm not scared for my own pay, but I watch the others.
fieldNote: Protective of **older colleagues**, and offers to teach Gill rather than compete.
Plans to move towards the **people side** of housing work.
Family is a quiet safety net: she would lean on parents for rent.

steps.text: Volunteer to test the invoice-reading tool with Marcus
Press on with the accounting qualification
Ask about a move into tenant services
Show Gill the tool in my lunch break

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the board needs to meet this month and agree no one is cut without a plan. To friends I'd say this is when governments must step in with a retraining guarantee or basic income. Online I'd share petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think my whole profession is on a clock. Two years is nothing. By the time I finish the accounting qualification, the work it's for might be done by software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the course and put the money into savings, about five hundred a month. I'd join the union branch properly. And I'd move towards tenant-facing work, where a person in the room still matters. I'd also ask my parents whether the shop could use me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be fine this year, because I have savings and my parents, but I'd watch the news every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years not leave time for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't leave time to qualify, or to find out if the tenant work is real. With five years I'd train for something. With two, I can only protect what I have and ask for help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop the course. Isn't that giving up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like it. But paying for study that might not pay back is a risk I can't take when I'm the first in my family in an office job. My dad would say save the money, and he'd be right.

say: I'd say the board must meet this month and agree **no cuts** without a plan.
I'd tell friends governments must offer a **retraining guarantee** or basic income.
think: Two years is nothing: the work my **qualification** is for might be software's by the time I finish.
I can only protect what I have and ask for help.
do: Stop the course and save about **£500 a month**.
Move towards tenant-facing work and ask my parents about the shop.
feel: **Anxious**; fine this year thanks to savings, but watching the news every night.
S2.quote: With five years I'd train for something. With two, I can only protect what I have and ask for help.
fieldNote: Stops study rather than gamble **money** on a qualification that may not pay back.
Sees being first in her family in an office job as a reason for caution.
Turns to **people-facing work** and family when time runs short.

steps.text: Stop the accounting course and save 500 pounds a month
Join the union branch and go to its meetings
Ask about tenant-facing roles at the association
Ask my parents whether their shop could use me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say five years is long enough to redesign roles around people, if we start now. To friends I'd say it's a warning shot for politicians. Online I'd write a longer post about a fair share of the gains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd think I have time to make myself useful in a way a machine isn't, like dealing with tenants in trouble. But I'd have to move early. The people who wait lose first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the tenant support team within a year. I'd keep the accounting course going part time, in case the money skills matter, and keep saving three hundred a month. I'd also teach Gill and the others the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. Five years feels long enough to make a decent plan without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me try the new role and go back if it doesn't suit. In two years I'd have no room to try. Five years also lets my parents wind the shop down on their own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the housing association itself shrinks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on my savings and my parents for a few months and look at councils or charities. Public jobs rely on people, not just paperwork, so I'd hope they hold on longer. It's a hope, not a promise.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to **redesign roles** around people.
I'd call it a warning shot for politicians and write about a **fair share** of the gains.
think: I can make myself useful in a way a machine isn't, such as helping **tenants in trouble**.
Moving early matters, because the people who wait lose first.
do: Move into the **tenant support team** within a year.
Keep the accounting course going part time and save **£300 a month**.
Teach Gill and others the tools.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**; five years feels long enough for a plan without panic.
S3.quote: The people who wait lose first.
fieldNote: Longer warning lets her **try and go back**, which two years would not.
Counts on councils and charities as a fallback, but calls it a hope, not a promise.
Wants to **share skills** with colleagues, not out-run them.

steps.text: Move into the tenant support team within the year
Keep the accounting course going part time
Keep saving 300 pounds a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say ten years is a long runway and we should use it to rethink how housing is paid for. To friends I'd say start talking about shorter weeks now. Online I'd keep it light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel okay. I'd be thirty-two, with a career built on the people side and ten years of savings. I'd be curious how it changes housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the accounting qualification, since that's a long game, and learn the AI tools as they improve. I'd save for a flat deposit and take on tenant work. I'd also help my parents sort out the shop's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years gives a person time to be sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children, if you have them by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn how people work, not only how software works. I'd want them to be curious and kind, and to know a trade or a craft too, because those hold their value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Who gets the gains. If a few companies own the AI and everyone else rents it, a calm ten years could turn into an unfair one. That's a political question, and I'd vote and campaign on it.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** to rethink how housing is funded.
I'd start the talk about **shorter weeks** now but keep it light online.
think: I'd be thirty-two with a **people-side career** and savings, so I feel okay.
I'm curious, not frightened, about how housing changes.
do: Finish the **accounting qualification** and learn AI tools as they improve.
Save for a **flat deposit** and take on tenant work.
Help my parents plan the shop's future.
feel: **Calm**, mostly; ten years gives time to be sensible.
S4.quote: Who gets the gains. If a few companies own the AI and everyone else rents it, a calm ten years could turn into an unfair one.
fieldNote: The long runway makes her **calm**, with her concern moved to fairness.
Plans in layers: qualification, **tenant work**, deposit and family.
Politics is her outlet, through votes and campaigning.

steps.text: Finish the accounting qualification

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years leaves no room to try anything, and I'd end up protecting what I have. A retraining guarantee, with pay while I study, would help, and a union at the table when firms bring tools in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm lucky, and I know it. Not everyone has parents who can catch them, and nobody should need parents to.

headlineQuote: Not everyone has parents who can catch them, and nobody should need parents to.
portrait: Beth is a **22-year-old finance assistant** at a Bristol housing association, top of her class with no debt.
She uses AI **now and then** and moves when change is proven, not before.
She blames **weak public support**, not technology, and leans on unions and government.
Her mood rises and falls with the clock: **uneasy, then anxious** at two years, calm at ten.
She is aware that **family backing** is what separates her from others.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries her most, because two years leaves no time to try a new path.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining guarantee** with pay while she studies.
A **union at the table** whenever firms bring in new tools.
